name: Electrostatic and gravitational fields of force

statementText.2.6-a: the features of electric and gravitational fields as specified in the table on page 30 [Table, two columns, ELECTRIC FIELDS | GRAVITATIONAL FIELDS: Electric field strength, E, is the force per unit charge on a small positive test charge placed at the point | Gravitational field strength, g, is the force per unit mass on a small test mass placed at the point; Inverse square law for the force between two electric charges in the form F = (1/(4πε₀)) Q₁Q₂/r² (Coulomb's law) | Inverse square law for the force between two masses in the form F = GM₁M₂/r² (Newton's law of gravitation); F can be attractive or repulsive | F is attractive only; E = (1/(4πε₀)) Q/r² for the field strength due to a point charge in free space or air | g = GM/r² for the field strength due to a point mass; Potential at a point due to a point charge in terms of the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point | Potential at a point due to a point mass in terms of the work done in bringing a unit mass from infinity to that point; VE = (1/(4πε₀)) Q/r and PE = (1/(4πε₀)) Q₁Q₂/r | Vg = −GM/r and PE = −GM₁M₂/r; Change in potential energy of a point charge moving in any electric field = qΔVE | Change in potential energy of a point mass moving in any gravitational field = mΔVg; Field strength at a point is given by E = − slope of the VE – r graph at that point | Field strength at a point is given by g = − slope of the Vg – r graph at that point; Note that 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9 × 10⁹ F⁻¹ m is an acceptable approximation | (blank)]
statementText.2.6-b: the idea that the gravitational field outside spherical bodies such as the Earth is essentially the same as if the whole mass were concentrated at the centre
statementText.2.6-c: field lines (or lines of force) giving the direction of the field at a point, thus, for a positive point charge, the field lines are radially outward

statementText.3.8-c: how to calculate binding energy and binding energy per nucleon from given masses of nuclei
statementText.3.8-d: the conservation of mass / energy to particle interactions – for example: fission, fusion
statementText.3.8-e: the relevance of binding energy per nucleon to nuclear fission and fusion making reference when appropriate to the binding energy per nucleon versus nucleon number curve

statementText.3.9-a: how to determine the direction of the force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field
statementText.3.9-b: how to calculate the magnetic field, B, by considering the force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field i.e. understand how to use F = BIl sin θ
statementText.3.9-c: how to use F = Bqv sin θ for a moving charge in a magnetic field
statementText.3.9-d: the processes involved in the production of a Hall voltage and understand that VH ∝ B for constant I
statementText.3.9-e: the shapes of the magnetic fields due to a current in a long straight wire and a long solenoid
statementText.3.9-f: the equations B = μ₀I/(2πa) and B = μ₀nI for the field strengths due to a long straight wire and in a long solenoid
statementText.3.9-g: the fact that adding an iron core increases the field strength in a solenoid
statementText.3.9-h: the idea that current carrying conductors exert a force on each other and to predict the directions of the forces
statementText.3.9-i: quantitatively, how ion beams of charged particles, are deflected in uniform electric and magnetic fields
statementText.3.9-j: the motion of charged particles in magnetic and electric fields in linear accelerators, cyclotrons and synchrotrons
statementText.3.9-P1: Specified practical: Investigation of the force on a current in a magnetic field
statementText.3.9-P2: Specified practical: Investigation of magnetic flux density using a Hall probe

statementText.3.10-a: the definition of magnetic flux as φ = AB cos θ and flux linkage = Nφ
statementText.3.10-b: the laws of Faraday and Lenz
statementText.3.10-c: how to apply the laws of Faraday and Lenz (i.e. emf = - rate of change of flux linkage)
statementText.3.10-d: the idea that an emf is induced in a linear conductor moving at right angles to a uniform magnetic field
statementText.3.10-e: qualitatively, how the instantaneous emf induced in a coil rotating at right angles to a magnetic field is related to the position of the coil, flux density, coil area and angular velocity

statementText.3.A-a: using Faraday's law, the principle of electromagnetic induction applied to a rotating coil in a magnetic field
statementText.3.A-b: the idea that the flux linkage of a rotating flat coil in a uniform magnetic B-field is BAN cos ωt because the angle between the coil normal and the field can be expressed as θ = ωt
statementText.3.A-c: the equation V = ωBAN sin ωt for the induced emf in a rotating flat coil in a uniform B-field
statementText.3.A-d: the terms frequency, period, peak value and rms value when applied to alternating potential differences and currents
statementText.3.A-e: the idea that the rms value is related to the energy dissipated per cycle, and use the relationships I = I₀/√2 and V = V₀/√2, (including Vrms = ωBAN/√2)
statementText.3.A-f: the idea that the mean power dissipated in a resistor is given by P = IV = I²R = V²/R where V and I are the rms values
statementText.3.A-g: the use of an oscilloscope (CRO or PC based via USB or sound card) to measure • a.c. and d.c. voltages and currents • frequencies
statementText.3.A-h: the 90° phase lag of current behind potential difference for an inductor in a sinusoidal a.c. circuit
statementText.3.A-i: the idea that XL = Vrms/Irms is called the reactance, XL, of the inductor, and to use the equation XL = ωL
statementText.3.A-j: the 90° phase lead of current ahead of potential difference for a capacitor in a sinusoidal a.c. circuit, and to use the equation XC = Vrms/Irms, where XC = 1/(ωC)
statementText.3.A-k: the idea that the mean power dissipation in an inductor or a capacitor is zero
statementText.3.A-l: how to add potential differences across series RC, RL and RCL combinations using phasors
statementText.3.A-m: how to calculate phase angle and impedance, Z, (defined as Z = Vrms/Irms for such circuits)
statementText.3.A-n: how to derive an expression for the resonance frequency of an RCL series circuit
statementText.3.A-o: the idea that the Q factor of a RCL circuit is the ratio VL/VR (= VC/VR) at resonance
statementText.3.A-p: the idea that the sharpness of the resonance curve is determined by the Q factor of the circuit

statementText.3.B-a: the nature and properties of X-rays
statementText.3.B-b: the production of X-ray spectra including methods of controlling the beam intensity and photon energy
statementText.3.B-c: the use of high energy X-rays in the treatment of patients (therapy) and low energy X-rays in diagnosis
statementText.3.B-d: the equation I = I₀ exp(−μx) for the attenuation of X-rays
statementText.3.B-e: the use of X-rays in imaging soft tissue, and fluoroscopy to produce real time X-rays using image intensifiers
statementText.3.B-f: techniques of radiography including using digital image receptors
statementText.3.B-g: the use of a rotating beam X-ray computed tomography (CT) scanner
statementText.3.B-h: the generation and detection of ultrasound using piezoelectric transducers
statementText.3.B-i: scanning with ultrasound for diagnosis including A-scans and B-scans incorporating examples and applications
statementText.3.B-j: the significance of acoustic impedance, defined by Z = cρ for the reflection and transmission of sound waves at tissue boundaries, including the need for a coupling medium
statementText.3.B-k: the use of the Doppler equation Δf/f₀ = (2v/c) cos θ to study blood flow using an ultrasound probe
statementText.3.B-l: the principles of magnetic resonance with reference to precession nuclei, resonance and relaxation time, and to apply the equation f = 42.6 × 10⁶ B for the Lamour frequency
statementText.3.B-m: the use of MRI in obtaining diagnostic information about internal structures
statementText.3.B-n: the advantages and disadvantages of ultrasound imaging, X-ray imaging and MRI in examining internal structures
statementText.3.B-o: the effects of α, β, and γ radiation on living matter
statementText.3.B-p: the Gray (Gy) as the unit of absorbed dose and the Sievert (Sv) as the unit of equivalent dose and effective dose. Define absorbed dose as energy per kilogram
statementText.3.B-q: the use of the equations • equivalent dose = absorbed dose × (radiation) weighting factor H = DWR and • effective dose = equivalent dose × tissue weighting factor E = HWT
statementText.3.B-r: the uses of radionuclides as tracers to image body parts with particular reference to technetium-99m (Tc-99m)
statementText.3.B-s: the use of the gamma camera including the principles of the collimator, scintillation counter and photomultiplier / CCD
statementText.3.B-t: positron emission tomography (PET) scanning and its use in detecting tumours

name: The physics of sports
option: Option C: The physics of sports

statementText.3.C-a: how to use the centre of gravity to explain how stability and toppling is achieved in various sporting contexts
statementText.3.C-b: how to use the principle of moments to determine forces within • various muscle systems in the human body and • other sporting contexts, for example, sailing
statementText.3.C-c: how to use Newton’s 2nd law in the form Ft = mv − mu in various sporting contexts
statementText.3.C-d: the coefficient of restitution as e = (Relative speed after collision)/(Relative speed before collision) and also use it in the form e = √(h/H) where h is the bounce height and H is the drop height
statementText.3.C-e: what is meant by the moment of inertia of a body
statementText.3.C-f: how to use equations to determine the moment of inertia, I, for example • a solid sphere I = (2/5)mr² • a thin spherical shell I = (2/3)mr² where m is the mass and r is the radius
statementText.3.C-g: the idea that angular acceleration, α, is defined as the rate of change of angular velocity, ω, and how to use the equation α = (ω₂ − ω₁)/t
statementText.3.C-h: the idea that torque, τ, is given as τ = Iα
statementText.3.C-i: angular momentum, L, is given as L = Iω where ω is the angular velocity
statementText.3.C-j: the principle of conservation of angular momentum and use it to solve problems in sporting contexts
statementText.3.C-k: how to use the equation for the rotational kinetic energy, rotational KE = ½Iω²
statementText.3.C-l: how to use the principle of conservation of energy including the use of linear and rotational kinetic energy as well as gravitational and elastic potential energy in various sporting contexts
statementText.3.C-m: how to use projectile motion theory in sporting contexts
statementText.3.C-n: how to use Bernoulli’s equation p = p₀ − ½ρv² in sporting contexts
statementText.3.C-o: how to determine the magnitude of the drag force using FD = ½ρv²ACD where CD is the drag coefficient

name: Energy and the environment
option: Option D: Energy and the environment

statementText.3.D-a: how the following affect the rate at which the temperature of the Earth rises including: (i) the need for thermal equilibrium: that is the balance between energy inflow from the Sun and energy re-radiated from the Earth in the context of global energy demand and the effect of CO₂ levels in the atmosphere (ii) the origin and means of transmission of solar energy and the form of the Sun’s power spectrum including the idea that wavelengths are converted into the near infrared in the atmosphere (iii) the use of Wien’s law (λmax T = constant) and Stefan-Boltzman T⁴ law in the context of solar power (iv) use of the density equation and Archimedes’ principle to explain why rising sea levels are due to melting ice caps and that the melting of ice on land increases sea levels but melting icebergs do not
statementText.3.D-b: the common sources of renewable and non-renewable energy and be able to compare their development and use both in the UK and internationally (i) solar power: • the idea that the main branch of the proton-proton chain is the main energy production mechanism in the Sun • the intensity of power from the Sun I = P/A and the inverse square law for a point source • how to perform energy conversions using photovoltaic cells (including efficiency calculations) (ii) wind power: • the power available from a flowing fluid = ½Aρv³ • the factors affecting the efficiency of wind turbines (iii) tidal barrages, hydroelectric power and pumped storage: • the principles of energy conversion (Ep to Ek) in tidal barrage, hydroelectric and pumped storage schemes and be able to carry out energy and power calculations related to these schemes and compare with the energy produced from wind (iv) nuclear fission and fusion: • the principles underlying breeding and enrichment in nuclear fission applications • the difficulties in producing sustained fusion power - fusion triple product
statementText.3.D-c: the principles of fuel cell operation and the benefits of fuel cells particularly regarding greenhouse gas emissions
statementText.3.D-d: the thermal conduction equation in the form ΔQ/Δt = −AK Δθ/Δx
statementText.3.D-e: the effect of insulation on thermal energy loss and be able to calculate the heat loss for parallel surfaces using the rate of energy transfer = UAΔθ including cases where different materials are in contact
